entries.title: Oregon school shooting: 3 children, teacher killed; 16-year-old gunman dies after community member pursues him into school
entries.summary: A 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, and wounded two others. A community member pursued and killed the suspected shooter, authorities said.
entries.content:
October 15, 2026

A 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, and wounded two others. A community member pursued and killed the suspected shooter, authorities said.

A 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher and wounded two others in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday before a community member pursued and killed him, authorities said.

"The deceased at the scene include three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and one teacher," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters. Another child and a teacher were injured and taken to a hospital.

The first 911 call came in around 1 p.m. local time (2000 GMT) from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone carrying a long gun, Krantz said.

Additional 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said. Officers arrived within minutes.

"Seconds later, we received word over the radio that the suspect in this incident was down," Miller said.

Students evacuated as police respond to shooting

Bend is a ​city of some ‌100,000 people in central Oregon, about 175 miles (280 kilometers) southeast of Portland.

An updated post later said law enforcement was escorting students by bus to a separate location, where they could reunite with their families. The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly children aged ⁠5 to ​11. It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Miller said.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek thanked the community member who "heroically intervened to ​stop further loss of life."

"No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have ​to live through ‌this kind of day. And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to ‌cry privately," Kotek said.

US grapples with recurring mass shootings

The United States, where firearms are widely available, experiences frequent gun violence, with thousands of people killed each year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among high-income countries.

The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007. South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.

There have been more than 365 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, excluding the shooter.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Bus, train collide, injuring 19 at Channel Tunnel terminal
entries.summary: A minibus carrying truck drivers collided with a freight train near the Channel Tunnel entrance in France, injuring 19 people, two of them severely. Authorities launched an inquiry into what caused the accident.
entries.content:
France

Bus, train collide, injuring 19 at Channel Tunnel terminal

October 15, 2026

A minibus carrying truck drivers collided with a freight train near the Channel Tunnel entrance in France, injuring 19 people, two of them severely. Authorities launched an inquiry into what caused the accident.

A minibus collided with a stationary train near the entrance to the Channel Tunnel in northern France on Thursday, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, authorities said.

Two people, including the bus driver, were seriously injured and airlifted to a hospital in Lille, but none of the injuries were life-threatening, the local prefect said, revising down earlier reports of five people seriously injured passengers. The other injured passengers were brought to nearby hospitals for treatment.

The minibus was carrying truck drivers of various nationalities preparing to board a shuttle train through the tunnel. LeShuttle carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel.

Pas-de-Calais Deputy Prefect Agathe Cury said an inquiry was launched to determine what caused the accident.

"This is the first time an incident of this type has occurred" at a Eurotunnel loading platform, she said.

Eurostar and freight service to continue

Eurostar, which runs passenger train services between mainland Europe and the UK, said the collision would not impact its services.

"An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel tonight, not involving Eurostar. This incident does not impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected," the company said in a statement.

The last two trains between Paris and London were canceled. Eurostar said this was due to engineering work, not the accident.

The 50-kilometer (31-mile) Channel Tunnel is the longest infrastructure of its kind in the world. It has linked Coquelles in northern France and Folkestone in England since 1994. Operated by Getlink, the tunnel is used by several hundred trains every day.

Eurostar, which is a separate entity, has held a monopoly on cross-Channel passenger rail services for decades, said it carried 11.8 million passengers in 2025.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro pleads not guilty to torture charges
entries.summary: Maduro and his wife were charged with leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.
entries.content:
United States of America

Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro pleads not guilty to torture charges

October 15, 2026

Maduro and his wife were charged with leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.

Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro appeared in court on Thursday, where he rejected newly unsealed torture charges against him and his wife, Cilia Flores.

He said the indictment represented "false accusations" against him.

Maduro was combative in court as he was asked to enter a plea to the charges, condemning allegations of torture as "false accusations and false testimony."

Ultimately, Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein interjected to declare that "a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro."

Flores told the judge through the Spanish interpreter: "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty."

The court appearance was the latest for the pair, who are currently in US custody in New York City, now eight months since they were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a nighttime raid.

The new torture charges against the couple have been added to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced.

Maduro and Flores' trial is set to begin June 14, 2027, according to a schedule approved by the judge Thursday.

What are the torture charges?

Maduro and his wife have been accused of leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans, during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.

They are said to have committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.

Security forces have been accused of torturing prisoners with electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.

Maduro stands accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims' treatment, and threatening to kill one prisoner's child as a form of psychological torture.

For her part, Cilia Flores has been accused of helping develop the repressive system and ordering the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.

Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but the US indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

Maudro has been under investigation by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents, but the court has not served him with a warrant.

Torture is considered a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside of the nation where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims' nationality.

But in the US, the prosecution of foreign officials is exceedingly rare. The only recent cases include the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad's Syria.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Self-replicating AI: Is your fridge a cybersecurity risk?
entries.summary: Anthropic researchers warn that AI worms could soon target connected household devices and spread from one device to another. Cyberattacks on French supermarkets illustrate just how vulnerable such systems can be.
entries.content:
October 15, 2026

Anthropic researchers warn that AI worms could soon target connected household devices and spread from one device to another. Cyberattacks on French supermarkets illustrate just how vulnerable such systems can be.

In the living room, a robot vacuum cleaner moves back and forth, the lights are dimmed by voice assistants, the heating is controlled via smartphone and the TV connects to the  internet to access a favorite streaming service. These are all examples of the "Internet of Things," in which connected electronic devices exchange data and communicate with one another.

According to recent market research by industry association Bitkom, about half of all households in Germany use such or similar "smart home" applications — and the figure is rising.

Now, the artificial intelligence company Anthropic has published a report warning that AI-powered malware could soon infiltrate connected household devices, copy itself to other devices and become active there.

Computer viruses that copy themselves from one machine to another have existed for decades. They are also known as worms and follow a predefined sequence of instructions. They exploit known security vulnerabilities or poorly protected access points. However, once the vulnerabilities are patched up or suitable attack vectors are no longer available, a worm can no longer spread so easily.

AI worms, however, would be far more complex and potentially much more harmful. They could solve problems autonomously and adapt to different devices, for example by coping with a different operating system or limited memory. They might also figure out for themselves how to operate on other devices or identify and circumvent new security updates

Spreading via TVs

Anthropic researchers investigated whether AI models could also run on relatively inexpensive hardware. In an experiment, they distributed an AI model across 15 low-cost Android TV boxes, with each device handling part of the computation. This demonstrated that certain AI applications can run without a large data center.

In a controlled test environment, the researchers set up eight additional simulated Android devices. The AI model was able to infiltrate one of them, replicate itself and infect other devices. In four out of five attempts, it reached all eight target devices. In the remaining attempt, it reached seven of the eight.

If equipped with malware, such an AI model could potentially adapt relatively quickly to previously unknown environments and disrupt processes and operations. It could learn to circumvent various security measures rather than simply exploiting a single vulnerability. According to Anthropic's developers, this sort of "AI worm" could take roughly one to two days to establish itself on a new, previously unknown device.

A botnet of household devices?

One particularly worrying possibility is that AI could link the infected devices into a large botnet. A single infected device has limited computing power, but the more devices are compromised, the faster the AI worm could spread. The malware would no longer depend on a central server that could simply be shut down.

It might also continuously learn as it spreads. It is conceivable that it could jump to entirely different types of electronic devices, all running different software.

Infected devices could be disconnected from the network and security vulnerabilities could still be patched. The malware's decentralized structure, however, would make it difficult to contain. Anthropic itself compares this potential development to a digital slime mold slowly spreading.

Researchers at Anthropic deliberately made access to the test devices very easy and left out major digital safeguards. Even so, the company believes smaller AI models could reach the necessary level of capability later this year to spread in the real world.

Overheating cooling systems

The potential consequences of cyberattacks on connected control systems has already been seen in an incident in France. Overnight into Monday, attackers tampered with refrigeration and freezer systems at numerous supermarkets. Temperatures in the affected units rose to as high as 50 degrees Celsius. Food spoiled, and some incidents also involved fires and technical damage.

France's cybersecurity agency, CERT-FR, initially confirmed that remote-control systems made by Danish manufacturer Danfoss had been compromised. The warning was later extended to systems made by other manufacturers. Investigations into the circumstances of the attack are ongoing.

Modern supermarkets use digital controllers to monitor and regulate refrigeration systems. Maintenance companies can access these systems remotely, for example to check temperatures. However, some of the security software was reportedly outdated, which the attackers may have exploited as an entry point for their cyberattack.

A new dimension in cyberattacks?

It remains unclear who was behind the attacks in France and what motivated them. There is also no evidence so far that a self-replicating AI worm was used in the attacks on French refrigeration systems. However, Anthropic's latest research shows how significantly AI could facilitate the development of malware, potentially enabling attacks on connected devices with serious consequences and without requiring much computing power.

Fearing further attacks, France's cybersecurity agency advised all companies to update their connected devices regularly, install essential security patches and, where possible, to disable unnecessary internet access altogether.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Middle East updates: Houthis target Yemen government palace in Aden
entries.summary: Houthi rebels say they targeted Saudi military assets in a rare attack on the interim seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. Meanwhile, vessels are again under fire near the Strait of Hormuz. More on DW.
entries.content:
Middle East

Middle East: Houthis target Yemen government palace in Aden

Published October 15, 2026last updated October 16, 2026

Houthi rebels say they targeted Saudi military assets in a rare attack on the interim seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. Meanwhile, vessels are again under fire near the Strait of Hormuz. More on DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Two guards killed in Houthi strike on Yemen port city of Aden
  • Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and cabinet officials were unharmed in the attack targeting the government palace
  • Iran reports tanker on fire in Gulf of Oman

Follow our roundup of headlines on the Saudi-Houthi conflict, Iran war and other Mideast topics on Thursday, October 15.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Saudi-led coalition says missile intercepted over Medina

Saudi-led coalition says missile intercepted over Medina

Houthi rebels on Thursday denied having launched a missile attack towards the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest cities. Earlier, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a cruise missile over the province of Medina.

The Houthis have previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.

Also on Thursday, Saudi authorities said a drone was destroyed over a major oil-producing region in the Eastern province.

For weeks, a Saudi-led coalition and Yemeni government forces have been fighting off a resurgence of Iran-backed Houthi rebels, who have recently made territorial gains along Yemen's strategic Red Sea coastline. The Houthis have been escalating the conflict, including by targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said that in October, 20 separate Houthi attacks have targeted King Khaled International Airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, killing 17 people. Service at the airport was suspended this week.

Most of those fatalities came last Saturday, after a strike hit the airport, killing 13 people and wounding around 300 others, in the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade.

The UN Security Council on Thursday issued a statement condemning "in the strongest terms" the ongoing Houthi attacks, calling the strikes on civilian airports and other facilities "reckless."

Skip next section Saudi-led coalition command center hit by Houthi strike on Aden

Saudi-led coalition command center hit by Houthi strike on Aden

A Houthi missile strike on Yemen's southern port city of Aden on Thursday targeted command centers of a Saudi-led coalition and Yemeni government forces, an unnamed government minister told AFP news agency several hours after the attack.

Earlier reports said explosions were heard in the vicinity of the presidential palace in Aden, where Yemen's internationally-recognized government is based.

Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani, and cabinet officials, were unharmed, adding the attack had been carried out with five missiles. Two members of the prime minister’s security detail were reported killed.

Shorty after the attack, a Houthi-aligned television channel reported that a "military headquarters run by Saudi officers" was attacked.

Aden has been the interim seat of Yemen's government since Houthi rebels based in the north took over the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of northern Yemen in 2014.

A Saudi-led coalition is fighting the Iran-backed Houthis alongside government forces.

Skip next section Iran steps up attacks on shipping near Strait of Hormuz

Iran steps up attacks on shipping near Strait of Hormuz

Iran's military on Thursday said an oil tanker caught fire in the Gulf of Oman, just south of the Strait of Hormuz, while trying to pass through a "prohibited" area.

Although Iran did not directly claim responsibility for the tanker fire, state television cited an army statement saying an "offending" and "non-compliant" tanker had switched off its tracking system while trying to pass thought "the prohibited zone."

The US military, which is also enforcing a maritime blockade in the region, has not issued a statement.

The reported incident comes a day after Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said a cargo vessel was sunk while passing through Strait of Hormuz after striking a mine.

Iranian state media quoted the IRGC as saying the ship was sailing on an "unauthorized route," but did not share details of the vessel's identity or the fate of its crew. The state television report included footage of an unidentified ship listing and billowing a plume of smoke.

Meanwhile, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said a Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride was hit by "unknown projectiles" on Tuesday and sank.

US broadcaster CNN reported that the GFS Pride is the ship the IRGC claimed struck a mine, and cited expert assessment that a drone strike is likely what actually caused the sinking.

In a statement, the MPA said all crew members were evacuated from the ship.

The MPA also reported a second vessel, the GFS Giselle, was attacked by projectiles on Tuesday, and sustained damage but was able to reach safe anchorage.

"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law," the authority said. The US military has not commented.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported Wednesday that two container ships were struck on Tuesday by projectiles but sustained only minor damage.

According to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the GFS Pride is one of only two ships to have been sunk in the Strait of Hormuz out of 114 reported incidents since the US launched the war with Iran in February.  

Skip next section Houthis target Yemen government palace in Aden

Houthis target Yemen government palace in Aden

On Thursday, Houthi rebels said a missile attack targeted the Yemeni government's interim capital, Aden.

Witnesses cited by news agencies reported several explosions and smoke rising from the area around the al-Maashiq Palace following the rare attack on the headquarters of Yemen's internationally recognized government in the southern port city.

Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and members of the government were safe, according to Yemen's Information Ministry.

The ministry statement added two members of the prime minister's security detail were killed.

Other reports, citing government officials, said 10 people were injured. It is currently unclear if the palace itself was hit, or what the extent of damage could be.

Houthi-affiliated media reported the strikes targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them."

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya ​Saree said the strikes targeted what he called "Saudi ‌military operations headquarters in Aden," Reuters reported.

Yemen's civil war reignited in September as the Iran-backed Houthis launched a rapid offensive against government forces, capturing key territory along the Red Sea coast and expanding their control over swathes of territory on the Red Sea.

Since then both sides have regularly traded strikes. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, with several killed in separate attacks on Riyadh airport. 

Despite, Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and government counter-offensives, the group’s recent territorial gains have largely remained intact.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Tensions continue to escalate in the ongoing conflict between the Houthi rebels and Yemen's Saudi-backed government.

The Houthis claimed a strike on the presidential palace in Aden. Saudi Arabia also reported that it had intercepted a missile targeting Medina.

Meanwhile, attacks on shipping continue, with Iran reporting on oil tanker was on fire in the Gulf of Oman, coming a day after a cargo ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine.

Stay tuned for more with DW.

entries.title: Police raid the major pro-opposition Halk TV channel in Turkey
entries.summary: Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of an important pro-opposition television station on Wednesdazy, the day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu was set to start his defense against corruption charges.
entries.content:
Turkey

Police raid major pro-opposition Halk TV channel in Turkey

October 15, 2026

Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of an important pro-opposition television station on Wednesdazy, the day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu was set to start his defense against corruption charges.

On Wednesday morning, the live broadcast was halted, Halk TV's headquarters in the city of Istanbul were searched, and a new administrator was appointed by the government to run the media outlet. An arrest warrant was issued for the station's CEO, Cafer Mahiroglu, who currently lives in London. According to prosecutors, 11 people were arrested.

Turkey has faced criticism for years over restrictions on press freedom. Halk TV is one of the country's best-known opposition television stations and regularly broadcasts critical reports about Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Justice and Development Party (AKP). After the raid, journalists were initially prevented from entering the building. Pre-recorded programs were broadcast instead of live reports.

The timing is particularly sensitive: Halk TV was raided on the very day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoglu was scheduled to begin his defense against corruption charges in court. The channel has been an important source of information for those following the trial.

Imamoglu, who won the mayoral election in Istanbul in 2019 and remained in office until his arrest on March 19, 2025, is one of Erdogan's most significant rivals, considered a beacon of hope for the opposition. He is still expected to run for president in 2028. 

He is accused of establishing and running a criminal organization, as well as of various related financial crimes. Prosecutors are seeking a prison term of 2,352 years related to 142 charges. Imamoglu denies the allegations, arguing that the case is politically motivated.

Raid linked to investigation into Cafer Mahiroglu

Istanbul prosecutors said that the raid on Halk TV was linked to an investigation into its CEO Mahiroglu, who is accused of bribery, bid rigging and money laundering.

They said that arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people, on top of the 11 arrests. Assets belonging to companies allegedly linked to Mahiroglu were also seized and a trustee appointed to run the firms.

The opposition responded with sharp criticism of the police raid. Ozgur Ozel, the leader of the social democratic New Party (Yeni Parti) said it was a dark day for Turkey.

"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," Mahiroglu said.

"Showing solidarity with Halk TV means supporting the struggle for democracy in Turkey," Ozel said.

He added that "only dictators" would launch "a dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee […]" and criticized the fact that this had occurred on the day that Imamoglu was due to begin his defense.

Journalists' union slams raid

The Journalists' Union of Turkey (TGS) also condemned the raid on the platform X, describing it as arbitrary and arguing that the press was free and should not be censored.

Editor-in-chief Suat Toktas tried in vain to persuade the new state-appointed administrator to continue live broadcasts. In a video released by the TV channel, he said that what was happening was "illegal."

Halk TV began broadcasting on January 10, 2005 and its live broadcasts gained widespread attention particularly during the 2013 Gezi Park protests. Cafer Mahiroglu took over the station in 2020.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Trump says execution of Fort Hood shooter will not be livestreamed
entries.summary: Trump said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan can be viewed in person by families of the victims if they wish. The decision comes after bipartisan backlash regarding the Pentagon's plans to livestream the execution.
entries.content:
October 15, 2026

Trump said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan can be viewed in person by families of the victims if they wish. The decision comes after bipartisan backlash regarding the Pentagon's plans to livestream the execution.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will not be livestreamed.

The announcement comes after the Trump administration faced criticism from both Republicans and Democrats, as well as rights groups and many in the international community. Vice President JD Vance also said he would not watch such a livestream.

Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."

But the president added that "any very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."

Trump said he "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed." He noted that the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, "if they so choose."

Hasan's execution is scheduled for Deccember 3 at the US military prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

A slew of criticism

The public execution idea drew wide condemnation from lawmakers of both main US parties, Republicans and Democrats, including top House Republican Mike Johnson, who said it could be a "recruiting tool for future terrorists."

Dozens of retired US military officers also published an open letter warning against broadcasting the execution, saying it "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it."

The letter added that such a move woud "ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers," said the officers, including more than 40 generals and admirals.

Even Vice President JD Vance was reticent about the plan.

When asked about the public execution and whether it was acceptable in his Christian faith, Vance said he didn't know that it would actually happen.

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said, adding: “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it."

Hegseth had sought to make execution 'public'

The plan to livestream Hasan's execution was announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

In a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts, Hegseth had said that Hasan would get "a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."

Hasan was an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major when he carried out the shooting in a medical building on November 5, 2009.

Soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment at the time of the shooting. Hasan shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — as he opened fire on his fellow soldiers

He was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement. He now uses a wheelchair.

During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.

The last time the US military carried out a service member execution was in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Russia arrests Swedish national, claims he's Ukraine fighter
entries.summary: Russian intelligence agents have arrested a Swedish man they say led a Ukrainian drone unit. He was detained at Russia's western border and is accused of planning acts of terrorism and sabotage.
entries.content:
October 15, 2026

Russian intelligence agents have arrested a Swedish man they say led a Ukrainian drone unit. He was detained at Russia's western border and is accused of planning acts of terrorism and sabotage.

Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) on Thursday announced the arrest and detention of a Swedish national who, authorities say, fights for Ukraine.

What do we know so far?

The 35-year-old Swede, detained near Pskov on Russia's western border, has been charged with illegally entering the country and may face additional terrorism charges, FSB representatives said.

Russia claims to have secured documents proving that the man led a Ukrainian drone unit.

They are now investigating whether he could be charged with organizing terror attacks on behalf of Ukraine or other Western intelligence services.

According to the FSB, the man "entered the Russian Federation under the pretext of joining the ranks of the Russian armed forces with the aim of carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorist attacks on military installations."

The FSB also released a video that it claimed showed the man confessing that he had entered Russia to commit "terrorist attacks" and sabotage.

During the video the man spoke in English, saying that he was from Stockholm, had signed a contract with Ukraine's Defense Ministry and had received drone training. Russian state TV showed images of what it said was the man's contract with Ukraine.

The Pskov region borders Belarus, Estonia and Latvia — the latter two being EU and NATO member states — FSB officials did not specify where exactly the man had arrived from.

Sweden aware of incident, with no comment yet from Ukraine

The Swedish Foreign Ministry has said that it is aware of the situation but not involved.

Ukraine has not commented on the arrest.

On Tuesday, Russia arrested a Japanese journalist that Moscow accused of spying, a claim that Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi rejected.

Russia itself has been accused of hiring and deploying numerous individuals to commit acts of sabotage abroad or to recruit locals willing to do so — this, beyond the country's legions of malign cyber actors.

None of the claims made by Russia and the FSB on Thursday can be substantiated.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries as Zelenskyy says 'we're done'
entries.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will again attack Russian energy sites, as Moscow has ignored a claim by US President Trump that an "energy ceasefire" had been agreed. Russia reported two attacks on refineries.
entries.content:
Europe

Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries, Zelenskyy says

October 15, 2026

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will again attack Russian energy sites, as Moscow has ignored a claim by US President Trump that an "energy ceasefire" had been agreed. Russia reported two attacks on refineries.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday said that military strikes on Russian energy infrastructure would resume, despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.

In an interview with London's Financial Times (FT) newspaper, Zelenskyy said, "The block [on energy infrastructure attacks] is out. We're done."

The announcement came after Russia reported Ukrainian attacks on oil processing plants in Ryazan, where fire broke out, and Saratov.

Kyiv had refrained from making attacks to give Trump's "energy ceasefire" a chance for success.

On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised "vigorous [US] efforts to initiate the peace process," and claimed that by resuming attacks, Ukraine "is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators."

Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, for instance on Wednesday, when Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.

Trump calls renewed strikes a 'disgrace'

Trump said Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries were a "disgrace," in an interview to broadcaster Newsmax, published on Thursday.

Trump asserted that Zelenskyy was less willing than Putin to reach a compromise to end the war.

"I think they actually both would like to see it end. But I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin," he said.

Kyiv blasts dangerous lack of US intel

Ukraine had gone along with Trump's public proposal — despite not being notified of any "ceasefire" ahead of time — but it seemed to have helped little in the eyes of US leadership.

To that end, Zelenskyy railed against a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence information this week as well as the throttling of SpaceX Starlink satellite access for Ukraine's troops after Trump last week announced a number of decisions that have had adverse consequences for Ukraine.

The Ukrainian president said his country's military leaders had been warned that they would not be receiving US intelligence if they did not abide by Trump's "ceasefire."

Despite Ukraine's restraint, that withholding of intelligence was on full display this week when Kyiv was blindsided by Russian drones and missiles without any prior warning from the US.

"We will find a way out," said Zelenskyy of the situation as Ukraine's Western allies scramble to pick up the intelligence and defensive slack left by the US.

Zelenskyy said he would be willing to halt energy infrastructure attacks again but only if the US supplied Patriot interceptors that would allow Kyiv to down incoming the Russian ballistic missiles and drones that have been raining down on Ukraine since February 24, 2022.

Zelenskyy: Starlink throttling a question of US 'will'

Despite US claims that the Starlink situation was the result of a technical glitch, Zelenskyy told the FT, "It was not a technical problem, it was will."

SpaceX owner Elon Musk said the US owns and operates the Starshield military version of Starlink used by Ukraine, adding that he and his company had nothing to do with the issue.

The FT interview comes in the wake of Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil as well as his promise to buy "millions of barrels" of Russian diesel fuel amid high fuel prices caused by the US war with Iran.

The deal, just weeks from the US midterm elections, is unlikely to bring down oil prices. But it does extend a lifeline to Russian President Putin, allowing him to continue his illegal invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy and went so far as to call for him to be replaced this weekend.

Trump's sanctions actions fly in the face of nearly five years of allied political efforts to pressure Moscow to end its invasion.

Trump's actions have enraged NATO allies and European leaders, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, for one, calling the US agreement to purchase Russian diesel "a very risky decision."

Meloni pointed out that the spike in oil prices was clearly precipitated by Trump's war in Iran and that his dealings with Putin would result in the Russian leader continuing his invasion of Ukraine rather than ending it.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Can Kenya preserve the democratic space Raila Odinga fought for?
entries.summary: One year after the former prime minister's death, Kenyans are reflecting on his contribution to democracy and national reconciliation. Odinga's "handshakes" with his political rivals remain the subject of much debate.
entries.content:
Kenya

Can Kenya preserve the democratic space Raila Odinga fought for?

October 15, 2026

One year after the former prime minister's death, Kenyans are reflecting on his contribution to democracy and national reconciliation. Odinga's "handshakes" with his political rivals remain the subject of much debate.

AsKenya marks the first anniversary of Raila Odinga's death on Thursday, the former prime minister remains a towering figure. For many, he symbolizes the struggle for multiparty democracyand constitutional reforms. For others, his political alliances raise questions about compromise, opposition politics and the direction of the movement he built.

The question is not only how Kenya remembers Odinga — but whether the principles he championed can survive. "I want his legacy to live beyond the party," 20-year-old Nairobi resident Beatrice Chebet told DW.

Chebet said Odinga wanted a Kenya grounded in peace, democracy, constitutionalism and the rule of law. She said younger generations must carry those aspirations forward.

Odinga had a lasting effect on the experiences and political journey of younger Kenyans, Chebet said. "Some of us were Gen Zs," she said. "We did not know any form of multipartyism without reading Raila.”

Forged in struggle

Odinga's influence was shaped by decades of opposition politics, detentions and campaigns for democratic change. His role in the disputed 2007 presidential election placed him at the center of one of Kenya's most consequential political crises. The postelection violence killed more than 1,100 people and displaced hundreds of thousands.

A power-sharing agreement brokered with international mediation led by Kofi Annan, the former secretary-general of the United Nations, made Odinga prime minister in a coalition government with President Mwai Kibaki. The settlement also established a reform agenda, including constitutional change. Kenya adopted a new constitution in 2010, introducing a devolved system of government.

The security and intelligence strategist Byron Adera said Odinga's impact extended beyond electoral politics. "Raila was an institution that rocked institutions, bringing about lasting and very impactful institutional reforms for the betterment of Kenya," Adera told DW. He identifies constitutional reform and efforts to bring competing political interests together as important parts of Odinga's legacy.

Reconciliation also became one of the most contested aspects of Odinga's career. His "handshakes" of reconciliation with Kibaki in 2008 and President Uhuru Kenyatta in 2018 and cooperation with President William Ruto in 2024 illustrated his willingness to pursue political agreements with former rivals.

Supporters saw dialogue as a way to reduce tensions and advance national interests; critics questioned what such arrangements meant for an independent opposition. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has strongly criticized the political rapprochement between President William Ruto and the late Raila Odinga.

In May, Gachagua called the handshake process "nonsense" and said it had eroded Kenya's democracy by weakening the opposition's ability to hold the government accountable. His position offers a contrasting view of the alliances that shaped Odinga's later political years.

What happens to Odinga's ODM party?

The debate over Odinga's legacy is especially pressing within the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), the party he helped found and led for years.

Edwin Sifuna, a potential presidential candidate in the 2027 election, who describes Odinga as both his leader and friend, said the ODM's identity and direction had changed fundamentally. "We run the risk of losing our core support, people who believed in the ideals of ODM, because we were always the party of the people," Sifuna told DW.

Sifuna said Odinga's influence on national politics and public debate was greatly missed. His remarks point to a central challenge for ODM: whether it can preserve its identity and connection with ordinary Kenyans while navigating a changing political landscape. However, in a bid to keep the Odinga name in politics, Winnie Odinga, daughter of Raila Odinga, declared that she will run for Senator of Nairobi County in the 2027 election.

Chebet said Odinga's legacy would be measured by whether future generations continue to defend the principles associated with his political journey. Adera, meanwhile, emphasizes the lasting importance of institutional reform and building bridges.

Their perspectives highlight the tension at the heart of Odinga's legacy: a leader remembered for expanding democratic possibilities, but whose political compromises remain debatable. A year after his death, Odinga's influence is still visible in Kenya's political arguments, party divisions and public calls for democratic accountability.

The lasting test will be whether Kenya's institutions, political parties and younger generation can carry those principles forward — and whether the democratic space Odinga helped shape can endure beyond the man himself.

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu
